patterns.title: Site Repair
patterns.summary: Place new work where it can repair a damaged site while protecting what already works.

provenance.authors: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: Where should we put an extension without destroying the best part of the site?
Our site has a damaged corner and a much-loved garden.
Can new construction improve an existing neighborhood?
How do we decide what to keep before drawing a building?
The easiest building location would remove mature trees.
We want to improve a former industrial site without erasing its history.
What should a site survey include beyond the property boundary?
How do we avoid making a greenfield site worse?

visuals.alt_text: Plan marks established trees, a retained path and disturbed ground beside an existing building.
visuals.caption: Record what already supports life before choosing a building footprint.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Two site plans compare an addition in the valued garden with an addition repairing the disturbed edge.
visuals.caption: A smaller intervention on degraded ground can preserve the most useful existing place.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Axonometric fragment connects a retained wall, restored ground and an unobstructed pedestrian route.
visuals.caption: Repair includes connections and ground conditions, not only the new building.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

patterns.title: South Facing Outdoors
patterns.summary: Give useful outdoor places access to the sun appropriate to their climate and season.

provenance.authors: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: Our garden is in shade whenever we want to use it.
Where should an outdoor sitting area go on this site?
The sunny terrace is too hot in summer.
How can a northern-hemisphere building leave useful sun for its courtyard?
Does the same orientation advice work in the southern hemisphere?
How do we compare winter sun with summer shade?
Our building blocks the best outdoor space.
Should we prioritize morning sun or evening sun outside?

visuals.alt_text: Northern-hemisphere site plans place outdoor space north and south of a building.
visuals.caption: In a northern temperate climate, a building north of the garden can preserve useful southern exposure.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Seasonal section compares low winter sun and high summer sun with shading.
visuals.caption: Evaluate occupied hours and seasonal shade; a sunny plan alone cannot establish comfort.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Two outdoor seats offer shaded and sunny choices beside planting.
visuals.caption: Choice is more useful than forcing every visitor into the same exposure.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

sources.title: A Pattern Language, pattern 105; Alexander, Ishikawa, Silverstein and colleagues
Patronato de la Alhambra: The Court of the Lions

photographs.alt_text: A shaded pavilion and arcaded gallery face the bright open Court of the Lions at the Alhambra.
photographs.caption: Court of the Lions, Alhambra; Nasrid royal workshop under Muhammad V. The shaded gallery and open court offer different exposures within the same outdoor place.

patterns.title: Water-Sensitive Landscape
patterns.summary: Shape ground, planting and drainage as a connected system that holds and safely conveys rain.

provenance.authors: Patternverse editorial synthesis; source organizations credited in article
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: Rainwater runs straight off our site and floods the entrance.
Can planting help manage runoff from a roof?
Where should excess water go when a rain garden fills?
We want a greener courtyard without creating damp walls.
How do we make drainage visible and understandable?
Our paved schoolyard becomes a puddle after storms.
Can we reduce runoff without relying entirely on underground pipes?
What maintenance does a planted drainage area need?

visuals.alt_text: Site plan connects roof runoff, planted storage and a safe overflow route.
visuals.caption: Follow the whole water path, including the route taken when storage is full.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Ground section shows shallow storage separated from a building and accessible path.
visuals.caption: Store water where the soil, foundations and expected use can tolerate it.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Two rainfall states compare normal treatment and overflow during an exceptional storm.
visuals.caption: A landscape feature needs a failure route as well as an attractive everyday condition.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

sources.title: RIBA Sustainable Outcomes Guide (2019): Sustainable Water Cycle
AIA Framework: Design for Water

photographs.alt_text: An unplanted excavated drainage basin in front of a planted bioswale beside buildings and a path.
photographs.caption: Two bioswales—planted channels that receive runoff—at different stages. The excavated foreground reveals the basin shape; planting fills the completed bed beyond.

photographs.alt_text: A rectangular planted street bed sits beside a Brooklyn pavement and a row of blue rental bicycles.
photographs.caption: Dean Street, Brooklyn. A planted bioswale receives water at the street edge, fitting drainage into the space beside everyday routes and cycle parking.

patterns.title: Positive Outdoor Space
patterns.summary: Give outdoor space a legible shape and useful edges rather than leaving it as leftover ground.

provenance.authors: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: The space between our buildings feels like leftover land.
Why does one small square feel better than a much larger plaza?
How can we make an outdoor meeting place feel defined?
Our development has plenty of open space but nowhere people stay.
Can we shape a public space without enclosing every side?
Where should seating go in an irregular courtyard?
How do we distinguish a useful square from a traffic island?
The lawn around our building is hard to use.

visuals.alt_text: Figure-ground plans compare scattered blocks and a deliberately shaped square.
visuals.caption: Read the space itself as a figure, not only the buildings around it.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Outdoor plan uses a building, trees and low edges to define an open room.
visuals.caption: Enclosure can be partial and varied while leaving obvious ways through.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Two plans compare a circulation shortcut through seating and a route beside it.
visuals.caption: A good shape still needs compatible routes, activities and places to pause.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

photographs.caption: Place des Vosges, Paris; seventeenth-century royal square created under Henri IV. The continuous building edge frames the planted center.

photographs.alt_text: A continuous curved terrace at Royal Crescent faces an open green lawn with a clear building edge.
photographs.caption: Royal Crescent, Bath; John Wood the Younger. The curved frontage gives the lawn a clear edge while leaving it open to the wider landscape.

patterns.title: Arcades
patterns.summary: Make a sheltered walking edge that joins buildings to public life.

provenance.authors: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: People hurry past our building because there is no shelter.
Could a covered walkway make the street more usable?
How wide should a sheltered edge feel when people also stop there?
Our shopfront canopy does not connect to the next entrance.
How can a building offer shade without closing itself to the street?
We need a dry route between public rooms.
Can columns make a walking route confusing or inaccessible?
Why do some colonnades feel welcoming and others deserted?

visuals.alt_text: Axonometric portico shows a continuous sheltered walking route beneath a roof, with columns and a seat beside it.
visuals.caption: The arcade makes an intermediate territory between interior rooms and exposed public ground.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Plan distinguishes a continuous clear route from doors, columns and sitting pockets.
visuals.caption: Shelter works as public infrastructure only when the route remains usable.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Two sections compare a shallow decorative canopy and a sheltered occupied edge.
visuals.caption: Depth and orientation determine which weather the edge actually moderates.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

photographs.caption: Portico at the Sanctuary of the Madonna di San Luca, Bologna; built through several historical campaigns. Repeated columns and sheltered bays make the route easy to follow.

photographs.alt_text: A vaulted street portico in Bologna has a long clear walking line beside doors and an open square.
photographs.caption: Portico di Santo Stefano, Bologna. Doorways and places to pause sit beside the continuous sheltered walking route.

patterns.title: Entrance Transition
patterns.summary: Use a sequence of thresholds to make arrival legible, comfortable and socially appropriate.

provenance.authors: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: Our front door opens straight from a busy street into a quiet room.
How can visitors feel welcome without exposing private activities?
The entrance lobby feels like a barrier rather than a welcome.
Can a small porch improve arrival?
We need a place to wait before entering a shared home.
How do we make arrival comfortable in bad weather?
Visitors do not know when they have entered the private part of our building.
How can a threshold work without adding steps?

visuals.alt_text: Plan sequences street, sheltered threshold, entrance and interior room.
visuals.caption: Arrival can change in stages without becoming a long or exclusionary obstacle course.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Open-sided entrance drawing shows a sheltered landing and a continuous level route through a visible doorway into the interior.
visuals.caption: A threshold can be perceptible through enclosure and light while keeping movement step-free.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Two entrances compare direct exposure into a room and a screened intermediate place.
visuals.caption: Protect privacy without hiding the destination or making people wait in the route.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

photographs.caption: Red House, Bexleyheath; Philip Webb for William Morris, 1859–1860. The projecting entrance marks a place to arrive between garden and house.

photographs.alt_text: Broad stone steps cross the lower courtyard toward a recessed arched doorway at Haddon Hall.
photographs.caption: Haddon Hall. Courtyard, steps and recessed doorway give arrival depth. This historic sequence illustrates successive thresholds; its stepped approach needs a separate access assessment.

patterns.title: Building Edge
patterns.summary: Give the meeting of building and ground enough depth to support everyday occupation.

provenance.authors: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: Our building meets the pavement with a blank wall.
Where can people wait without blocking the entrance?
How can a ground-floor facade contribute to public life?
We need places to pause along a long building.
Residents want privacy but the street feels deserted.
Can a sheltered bench improve the edge of a community building?
Our setback has become unusable planting behind a fence.
How do we make the boundary between indoors and outdoors useful?

visuals.alt_text: Plan gives an edge depth through doors, windows and sitting pockets.
visuals.caption: A useful edge offers different ways to engage while keeping the passing route clear.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Spatial fragment separates the passing route from a sheltered sitting place beside the building, with private interior beyond the wall.
visuals.caption: Depth can mediate between public and private without forcing either to disappear.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Three frontage fragments compare a blank wall, a shallow setback and an occupied threshold.
visuals.caption: The amount of setback matters less than what it enables people to do.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

photographs.alt_text: Bologna street portico with columns toward the square and entrances along the sheltered inside edge.
photographs.caption: Bologna, Santo Stefano. Columns, doorways and the adjoining square give the edge depth for walking, entering and pausing.

patterns.title: Wings of Light
patterns.summary: Break a deep building into shallower wings when useful daylight and outdoor relationships justify it.

provenance.authors: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, Murray Silverstein, with Max Jacobson, Ingrid Fiksdahl-King and Shlomo Angel
provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: Too many rooms in our plan are far from an exterior wall.
Could a narrower building improve daylight?
Should we divide a deep building into wings?
Our courtyard barely brings light to the rooms around it.
How do we balance more daylight with more facade?
The floor plan has a dark central zone.
Can a school use several shallow wings without wasting circulation space?
Does a thin building always use less energy?

visuals.alt_text: Two axonometric building forms compare a deep block with shallow connected wings around an open garden, showing their different exposed edges.
visuals.caption: Shallower occupied zones put more rooms near exterior edges.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Section compares deep floor area and shallow rooms with useful sky exposure.
visuals.caption: Extra perimeter helps only if openings can see useful sky.
visuals.creator: Patternverse

visuals.alt_text: Massing comparison marks daylight opportunities and longer exposed perimeter.
visuals.caption: More facade is a real tradeoff; compare comfort, area and envelope together.

patterns.title: Courtyards Which Live

provenance.evidence_note: A design proposition to evaluate in context, not a universal performance or health guarantee.

example_user_queries: The courtyard looks attractive but nobody spends time there.
How can our school courtyard become part of everyday life?
Our enclosed garden is either too hot or too shaded.
People walk around the outside instead of using the central court.

Can a courtyard improve light without making rooms overlook each other?
We need a sheltered place for people to meet outdoors.
What makes a courtyard feel welcoming rather than trapped?
